analysis.one_liner: Repeals the Patriot Act and the FISA Amendments Act and requires warrants to surveil Americans.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to eight House committees, never got a hearing or a vote, and died when Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would repeal the USA PATRIOT Act and the FISA Amendments Act of 2008, the two main laws the government used after September 11 to conduct broad surveillance, and restore the stricter pre-2001 rules. It would bar the government from collecting information about any U.S. person under the foreign intelligence law without a warrant based on probable cause. It would also stop the government from forcing tech companies to build ways to break their own encryption, add technical experts to the secret surveillance court, require an annual audit of compliance, and protect intelligence employees and contractors who report waste or lawbreaking.
analysis.who_benefits: Every American who uses a phone or the internet. Their calls, messages, and online activity could no longer be gathered in bulk without a judge-approved warrant naming them. Tech companies would benefit because the government could not force them to weaken encryption. Intelligence workers and contractors who spot wrongdoing would gain a protected way to report it without being fired.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the USA PATRIOT Act and the FISA Amendments Act of 2008 and restores the laws that existed before them, ending the legal basis for bulk surveillance programs exposed in 2013.
Bars the government from acquiring any information about a U.S. person under the foreign intelligence law without a warrant based on probable cause.
Prohibits the federal government from requiring makers of electronic devices or software to build in mechanisms that let the government bypass encryption or privacy technology.

Lets intelligence community employees and contractors report waste, fraud, abuse, or lawbreaking in FISA-authorized programs to Congress or the Comptroller General, and makes retaliation against them punishable up to termination.
Requires the Comptroller General to audit the government's compliance with the surveillance law every year and report the results to Congress.
Allows the secret surveillance court to appoint special masters with technical expertise to advise it, and extends FISA judges' terms from 7 to 10 years.

analysis.who_pays: Federal intelligence agencies would lose the broad surveillance powers the two repealed laws gave them, and the private contractors that help run surveillance programs would lose that work. Phone and cable companies would still be required to help carry out court-ordered surveillance of specific targets.

drawbacks.text: Repealing the Patriot Act and FISA Amendments Act removes the surveillance tools intelligence officials said were needed to track suspected terrorists, and the bill would leave intelligence agencies working under narrower, pre-2001 authorities.

The bill preserves the government's ability to compel phone companies, landlords, and others to help conduct surveillance of a specific target in secret, so some compelled cooperation with surveillance continues even after repeal.
Auditing compliance with a law governing classified surveillance is difficult for an outside auditor like the Comptroller General, and a GAO review may not uncover secret programs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The privacy gains are large and concrete: a warrant requirement for collecting Americans' information, a ban on forced encryption backdoors, and real protection for whistleblowers. The cost is real too, since some counterterrorism surveillance would get harder, and the bill would keep compelling secret cooperation from companies even while repealing the laws most associated with abuse. On balance it would trade some investigative flexibility for much stronger protection of ordinary people's communications.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to eight different House committees and several subcommittees, but no committee ever held a vote on it, and it expired when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Rep. Rush Holt introduced the Surveillance State Repeal Act on July 24, 2013, three weeks after the USA PATRIOT Act, the FISA Amendments Act of 2008, and other laws became the focus of public debate over government surveillance programs.

The same day it was introduced, the Speaker referred it not just to the Judiciary Committee but to seven others as well, including the Intelligence, Armed Services, and Financial Services committees, meaning eight committees would each need to act on the parts in their jurisdiction.
Over the next seven weeks it was referred to six subcommittees, including the Crime subcommittee of Judiciary and the Communications subcommittee of Energy and Commerce.
No committee reported the bill, no hearing or markup vote is recorded, and the last action of any kind came on September 13, 2013, sixteen months before the Congress ended.
Ten House Democrats cosponsored the bill, and no Republican signed on.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The intelligence agencies and their contractors, which kept the broad surveillance authorities the bill would have repealed. Tech companies also did well, since the prohibition on forced encryption backdoors never became law they could rely on, leaving the issue open.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Intelligence agencies that kept their surveillance powers

sides.party_line_note: All ten cosponsors were House Democrats and the sponsor was a Democrat, but because no committee or floor vote ever happened, Republican members' positions were never put on the record.

industries.note: Repeal of the Patriot Act would end the legal basis for bulk collection programs that involved customer phone records. But the bill keeps the requirement that carriers, landlords, and others furnish assistance for court-ordered surveillance of specific targets in secret, so companies remain part of the surveillance system even after repeal.

industries.industry: Intelligence agencies and their private contractors
industries.note: The bill repeals the two laws authorizing broad surveillance programs and subjects retaliation against whistleblowers to termination, directly shrinking the agencies' legal powers and the contractor work that depends on them.
The bill prohibits the federal government from forcing manufacturers to build encryption-bypass mechanisms into their products, letting companies promise customers uncompromised security.
